concepts.description: Project columns and computed expressions from a table with SELECT, control duplicate rows and assign readable output column names.
learning_objectives: Project the required columns and expressions in a SELECT list.
Assign readable output names with column aliases.
Remove duplicate result rows with DISTINCT and state the cost of doing so.
Predict the result columns produced by SELECT * and by an explicit column list.

concepts.description: Filter source rows with a boolean WHERE predicate that combines comparison, range, membership and NULL-aware conditions.
learning_objectives: Build a WHERE predicate that keeps exactly the rows required by a specification.
Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT while respecting operator precedence.
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL instead of equality when NULL values are involved.
Explain why a predicate that compares with NULL yields unknown rather than true.

concepts.description: Combine rows from related tables with JOIN, writing correct ON predicates and selecting the join type that matches the required result.
learning_objectives: Translate a relationship between tables into a correct JOIN ... ON condition.
Choose an inner or outer join based on whether unmatched rows must be kept.
Diagnose unexpected duplicate rows caused by a one-to-many join key.
Join three or more tables without losing the intended row population.

concepts.description: Group rows into sets with GROUP BY and compute per-group aggregates such as counts, sums and averages.
learning_objectives: Group rows by one or more columns to produce one output row per group.
Apply aggregate functions to summarize each group.
Distinguish a grouping column from an aggregated expression in the SELECT list.
Explain how a NULL grouping key forms its own group.

concepts.description: Filter grouped results with HAVING, distinguishing group-level predicates from row-level WHERE conditions.
learning_objectives: Apply HAVING to keep only groups that satisfy an aggregate condition.
Choose WHERE for row filtering and HAVING for group filtering inside the same query.
Explain why a WHERE clause cannot reference an aggregate result directly.
Predict the difference in output when a predicate moves from WHERE to HAVING.

concepts.description: Compose queries with scalar, row, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries in the SELECT, FROM and WHERE clauses.
learning_objectives: Use a scalar subquery where a single computed value is required.
Compare IN, EXISTS and join formulations for the same filtering task.
Write a correlated subquery that references the current outer row.
Explain when a subquery in FROM acts as an independent derived table.

concepts.description: Model a problem domain as entities, attributes and relationships, then translate the model into a relational schema with keys.
learning_objectives: Identify entities, attributes and relationships from a written domain description.
Determine cardinality and participation constraints for each relationship.
Convert an ER model into tables with primary and foreign keys.
Detect modeling choices that would duplicate data or lose required relationships.

concepts.description: Evaluate relational schemas with functional dependencies and normal forms, and decompose them to reduce redundancy and update anomalies.
learning_objectives: Explain which update, insert and delete anomalies normalization is intended to prevent.
Derive candidate keys from a set of functional dependencies.
Decompose a relation into higher normal forms while preserving its dependencies.
Verify that a decomposition is lossless and does not fabricate rows.

concepts.description: Reason about functional dependencies, attribute closure and candidate keys as the theoretical basis for relational design.
learning_objectives: Determine whether a functional dependency is implied by a given set of dependencies.
Compute the attribute closure of a determinant.
Derive all candidate keys of a relation from its functional dependencies.
Use inference rules to simplify a dependency set without changing its closure.

concepts.description: Apply first normal form by keeping every attribute atomic and eliminating repeating groups from relational tables.
learning_objectives: Identify repeating groups and multivalued cells that violate first normal form.
Restructure a non-atomic table into rows whose attribute values are atomic.
Explain why storing lists in a single column complicates querying and constraints.
Distinguish the requirements of first normal form from those of higher normal forms.

concepts.description: Apply second normal form by removing partial dependencies of non-key attributes on part of a composite candidate key.
learning_objectives: Detect a partial dependency on part of a composite candidate key.
Decompose a relation in first normal form into second normal form.
Explain why second normal form is automatic when the key is a single attribute.
Verify that the resulting decomposition preserves the original information.

concepts.description: Apply third normal form by eliminating transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on other non-key attributes.
learning_objectives: Detect transitive dependencies among non-key attributes.
Decompose a second-normal-form relation into third normal form.
Compare third normal form with Boyce-Codd normal form for a given schema.
Explain the redundancy that a transitive dependency introduces.

concepts.description: Explain the semantics of INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, including predicates, constraints and transaction effects, without executing mutations in the learner sandbox.
learning_objectives: Describe how INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change table contents.
Predict which rows an UPDATE or DELETE affects from its WHERE predicate.
Explain how constraints can reject or cascade a data modification.
State why destructive DML is assessed conceptually rather than executed in the read-only sandbox.

concepts.description: Explain schema-definition statements, keys and constraints, and the effects of altering an existing table without executing DDL in the learner sandbox.
learning_objectives: Describe how CREATE TABLE declares columns, data types and constraints.
Distinguish primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys and CHECK constraints.
Predict the impact of an ALTER TABLE operation on existing rows.
Explain why schema changes are assessed conceptually in the read-only sandbox.

clos.title: Explain safe SQL data modification and schema definition
clos.description: Owner-approved knowledge assessment via MCQ and essay, with read-only SQL execution.

questions.prompt: Which command changes values in existing rows while preserving the table definition?
Which statement defines a table and its referential integrity constraint?

options.option_text: CREATE TABLE with a FOREIGN KEY

questions.prompt: For Department(dept_id, name) and Employee(employee_id, dept_id, salary), explain how DDL defines keys and referential integrity and how INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE modify data. Describe a targeted salary update, the risk of a missing WHERE clause, and how foreign keys constrain deleting a department. Explain why these statements are described here rather than executed in this read-only assessment sandbox.
questions.reference_answer: CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE defines structure, primary keys and a foreign key from Employee.dept_id to Department.dept_id. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing values and DELETE removes rows. A salary update uses a predicate identifying intended employees; omitting WHERE can update every row. A referenced department deletion is rejected unless its declared referential action permits it; do not assume cascading deletion. These are conceptual answers: learner sandbox execution accepts only read-only SELECT and rolls back, so it cannot run DML/DDL.

rubrics.criteria: No coherent distinction between DML and DDL or safe integrity reasoning
Identifies one command category but omits predicates or key integrity
Correctly distinguishes commands and targeted changes with a minor omission in referential integrity or sandbox restrictions
Correct DDL keys and foreign key, DML distinctions, targeted-update safety, declared deletion behavior and read-only assessment boundary

assessments.title: Read-only SQL and Database Knowledge Benchmark
assessments.description: SQL querying and relational foundations plus conceptual DML/DDL. The reviewed MCQ pool includes both knowledge topics. Mutating SQL is not executed. Adaptive 10 MCQ, 2 SQL and 1 essay in 60 minutes.
